stage_state.summary_md:
## Principle 1: Shared Company Culture and Values

### Depth: Communicating Across Levels

Designing with data aims to reduce reliance on “gut” decision making and can break hierarchical, top-down structures. Data literacy across the company invites discussion, challenge, and the possibility of being wrong. User data—from A/B tests, ethnographic research, prototypes, surveys, usability studies, and more—drives decisions with less risk than executive hunches.

An early paper by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield (2007), “Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO,” argued that data resolves conflicts without relying on rank or politics. John Ciancutti, former VP of Product Engineering at Netflix, described how data literacy across all roles became a source of freedom and innovation. Patty McCord, Netflix’s Chief Talent Officer for over 12 years, noted that a mechanism to measure whether you are doing the right thing for customers gives more people a voice in product development.

At Netflix, the data-driven approach was universally accepted—from CEO Reed Hastings and CPO Neil Hunt down to individual contributors. Even the CEO’s ideas were subjected to the same A/B testing rigor. When Reed had a strong product idea, he would dictate it on “his test cell” (the experimental group he backed), which was tested against other cells proposed by the product team. If his cell didn’t win, it didn’t launch. Upper management holding themselves to the same process reinforced the practice of subjecting ideas to grounded review through experimentation and accepting “failure” as a positive outcome.

Shifting to a data-aware framework requires examining how decisions have been made. If one or two individuals previously held decision-making power, they must recognize the value of user data, as their individual weight will diminish—just like any other opinion. Designers and product people should also check their own comfort with data reducing the weight of their personal opinions in the process.
